title: Vitamin D Supplementation and the Incidence of Fractures in ... - Springer
text: Vitamin D Supplementation and the Incidence of Fractures in the Elderly Healthy Population: A Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials Although a well-established component of bone metabolism, the efficacy and safety of vitamin D supplementation for the prevention of fractures in elderly healthy individuals is still unclear. To perform a meta-analysis comparing vitamin D supplementation with placebo and its contributions on fracture incidence. This meta-analysis was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO), under protocol CRD42023484979. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Central databases from inception to November 2023 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing vitamin D supplementation versus placebo in individuals with 60 years of age or more and without bone related medical conditions such as cancer and osteoporosis. Seven RCTs with 71,899 patients were included, of whom 36,822 (51.2%) were women. There was no significant difference in total fracture incidence (RR 1.03; 95% CI 0.93–1.14; p = 0.56; I2 = 58%) between groups or subgroups. However, women had an increased risk for hip fractures (164 vs. 121 events; RR 1.34; 95% CI 1.06–1.70; p = 0.01; I2 = 0%). There was no significant difference in non-vertebral fractures, osteoporotic fractures development, or falls (RR 1.02; 95% CI 0.94–1.12; p = 0.6; I2 = 47%; RR 0.97; 95% CI 0.87–1.08; p = 0.63; I2 = 0%; RR 1.01; 95% CI 0.97–1.04; p = 0.66; I2 = 55%, respectively). Vitamin D supplementation does not reduce the total fracture development rate in the elderly healthy population, and it may increase the incidence of hip fractures among elderly healthy women. This finding suggests refraining from prescribing high intermittent doses of vitamin D, without calcium, to individuals aged 60 or older with unknown vitamin D serum concentration or osteoporosis status and inadequate calcium intake. The relationship between serum vitamin D and fracture risk in the elderly: a meta-analysis Prescription of vitamin D was associated with a lower incidence of hip fractures Discover the latest articles, books and news in related subjects, suggested using machine learning. Routine assessments of 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D) levels are conducted in patients with osteoporosis, with the standard recommendation of vitamin D and calcium supplementation as part of the treatment of osteoporosis. The recommendations of the Endocrine Society for prevention disease differ depending on age. In healthy individuals aged 50 to 74 years, it suggests against routine 25(OH)D testing and vitamin D supplementation. However, for the population aged 75 years and older, it suggests empiric vitamin D supplementation with 600 IU daily for individuals aged 50 to 70 years, and 800 IU daily for those older than 70 years, for the potential decreased risk of mortality.5,6 However, the impact of vitamin D supplementation alone in primary prevention of fracture in elderly individuals without osteoporosis and hypovitaminosis D is a subject of controversy. For instance, two previous meta-analyses observed positive outcomes with vitamin D supplements (≥ 800 IU daily) in preventing hip and non-vertebral fractures in individuals aged 65 years and older,7 as well as its combination with calcium demonstrated a reduction in overall fractures and hip fractures.8 However, their conclusions may be influenced by participants residing in institutional settings. Conversely, other published meta-analyses demonstrated a neutral impact of vitamin D supplementation and the incidence of fractures.9,10 Therefore, we sought to perform an updated systematic review and meta-analysis examining the impact of vitamin D supplementation alone, without calcium, compared to placebo on fracture outcomes in healthy participants aged 60 years or more. We hypothesize that such supplementation does not prevent fractures in this population. Inclusion in this meta-analysis was restricted to studies that met all the following eligibility criteria: (1) randomized controlled trial; (2) comparing vitamin D in an average daily dose of 800 IU or higher with placebo (since that is the minimum dosage recommended for the main guidelines for that population3,6); (3) enrolling patients with more than 60 years old; (4) with follow-up with at least 12 months; and (5) included at least 500 participants, in order to minimize random error and publication bias. In addition, studies were included only if they reported fractures as the clinical outcomes of interest. We excluded studies that had (1) calcium supplementation on the intervention; (2) participants living in nursing homes; and (3) participants with medical conditions related with bone metabolism, such as cancer, osteoporosis, nephrolithiasis, sarcoidosis, or parathyroid disorders. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Central databases from inception to November 2023 with the main following search terms: “Vitamin D,” “supplementation,” “elderly,” “fracture,” and “randomized trial.” Search strategies used in each databases are presented in the Appendix. The references of all included studies and previous meta-analyses were also searched manually for any additional studies. Study triage against eligibility criteria was performed by two authors (M.S and R.D.). Disagreements were resolved through a consensus after discussing reasons for discrepancy. Two authors (M.S. and V.D.) independently extracted the data following predefined search criteria and quality assessment. Disagreements were resolved through a consensus after discussing reasons for discrepancy. The prospective meta-analysis protocol was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) on November 20th, 2023, under protocol CRD42023484979.
